studies.label: Study 2 (AI dependence manipulation, AUT with ChatGPT)

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Participants; actual sample reiterated under Sample size justification
counts_source.quote:
A total of 132 university students (including graduate students; 51 males,
81 females) were recruited and randomly assigned to either the high-dependence group
(n = 66) or the low-dependence group (n = 66).

arms.name: High AI dependence
arms.description: During priming, participants had to use ChatGPT answers for calculation, summarisation, and translation and were told AI answers were optimal. During the AUT, they used ChatGPT and were instructed to adopt its creative solutions directly (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.2).

arms.name: Low AI dependence
arms.description: During priming, participants completed the same tasks independently without external tools. During the AUT, they used ChatGPT as a supplementary reference and were instructed to complete final solutions independently (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.2).

studies.task: Generate as many innovative uses as possible for a tennis racket and a water pipe in an Alternative Uses Task framed as a creative competition.

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT (model version not stated)
ai_tool.locator: PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.2, Experimental design and procedure

estimates.outcome: AUT creativity index (Consensual Assessment Technique, mean of three raters)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Three psychology graduate students, trained in a calibration session and blind to condition, rated novelty, appropriateness, and fluency on seven-point Likert scales. The mean of the three raters’ scores was the creativity index. The paper does not fully describe aggregation across dimensions, ideas, or the two AUT objects (PDF p. 6, Section 3.2, Measures).

sources.locator: PDF p. 5, Section 3.2, Sample size justification
sources.quote:
The actual sample of 132 participants (66 per
group) exceeded this minimum, ensuring adequate power for detecting the hypothesised
group differences.

sources.locator: PDF p. 6, Table 2, Creativity row; columns High AI Dependence, Low AI Dependence, t(130), p, Cohen’s d; table note identifies parenthesized values as SDs

sources.quote: t(130) = 4.03, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 0.70, a medium-to-large effect size.

estimates.notes: Both arms used ChatGPT during the scored AUT. High dependence is the manipulated configuration and low dependence is supplementary-reference use, following the screening arm names and treatment direction. Table 2 and the prose print positive t and Cohen’s d for Low AI dependence minus High AI dependence, opposite to the treatment-minus-control direction of this record. Their printed signs are retained; do not interpret the positive paper effect as a benefit of the treatment. The paper does not state the denominator used for Cohen’s d. Arm SDs and the independent-samples test concern participant creativity scores, with raters averaged before comparison. Counts are the stated actual sample and per-group counts, not counts derived from degrees of freedom; no exclusions or separate outcome-specific analyzed counts are reported. The manipulation bundles prior task reliance/trust with the AUT use instruction. No standalone unadjusted mean difference or confidence interval is printed outside the mediation analysis, and none is calculated here.

not_extracted.what: S1: cross-sectional survey, including S1-O1 self-reported creativity and all survey associations
not_extracted.reason: No random assignment and no creativity scored on produced output. The article describes a cross-sectional survey and says the creativity scale measures self-perceived capacity rather than task performance (PDF p. 3, Sections 2.1-2.2).
Self-report manipulation check, not an outcome scored on creative output (PDF p. 6, Sections 3.2-3.3 and Table 2).
Questionnaire measured as in Study 1, not a scored output or a convergent test with correct answers (PDF p. 3, Section 2.2, Measures; PDF p. 6, Sections 3.2-3.3 and Table 2).
Self-report scale used as an alternative mediator, not an outcome scored on output (PDF p. 6, Section 3.2, Measures and Table 2).

not_extracted.what: S2: mediation analyses of critical thinking and self-efficacy, including path effects and mediator-adjusted creativity
not_extracted.reason: Mediation analyses and effects adjusted for post-treatment mediators are excluded by extraction rule 5. Their total/direct/indirect path quantities are not additional eligible estimates of the Table 2 contrast, and the indirect-effect interval is not an interval for the treatment contrast (PDF pp. 6-7, Section 3.3, Mediation analysis and Figure 3).

not_extracted.what: S3: thinking-orientation experiment, including S3-O1 AUT creativity
not_extracted.reason: Random assignment is stated, but random assignment to generative-AI assistance or different generative-AI configurations on the creative task cannot be confirmed. The described dependence manipulation concerns unnamed AI investment advice in a trust game; the subsequent AUT is called identical to Study 2 without stating AI availability or condition-specific AI instructions (PDF pp. 7-8, Section 4.2). The supplement needed to resolve this was unavailable. The full-sample creativity effects in Table 4 are therefore left unextracted pending clarification. Cell-specific simple effects, moderation, mediation, and questionnaire outcomes would also be excluded under rule 5 (PDF pp. 8-10, Section 4.3, Tables 3-5).

open_items: Study 3 eligibility remains unresolved: confirm whether generative AI was used during the AUT and whether AI availability or use instructions differed by randomized arm. The statement that the task was identical to Study 2 does not specify its AI conditions. Also identify the trust-game AI and clarify the setting (PDF pp. 7-8, Section 4.2).

The separately listed supplement contains task instructions and CAT rubrics (PDF p. 13, Supplementary Materials). Python urllib requests to https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/jintelligence14080168/s1 and the alternative https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13514692/fullTextXML used User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1; both failed with WinError 10013 (socket access forbidden). No supplementary content was read.
Study 2 does not name the ChatGPT model version or its release year; ai_tool.year is null (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.2).
The CAT procedure specifies averaging raters but does not fully explain aggregation over dimensions, multiple ideas, and AUT objects (PDF p. 6, Section 3.2, Measures).

The denominator used for the printed Cohen’s d is not specified. No SE or confidence interval for the eligible unadjusted creativity contrast is printed; participant arm means, SDs, and counts are available (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3 and Table 2).
notes: The complete markdown conversion was read from beginning to end, including end matter and references. The saved PDF contains no appendix; the external supplement was not available. All cited PDF pages were extracted with pymupdf and all retained numeric statistics were checked against PDF text; the Table 2 row is legible in extracted text. Only Study 2 is represented in studies and estimates. Study 1 is excluded and Study 3 is deferred rather than assigning unknown AI conditions by analogy. No separate diversity outcome is reported. The country is supported by the institution description in PDF p. 3 and the statement that all participants came from a single institution in PDF p. 12, Section 5.3. Preregistration is not stated anywhere in the saved article. The reconciled form lists no shared participant sample with another paper. No effects, standard errors, intervals, arm totals, or standardized quantities were computed. Printed precision is retained in source quotes.
